questions.q: Which of the following best describes a pressure group in Nigeria?
options: An organization that seeks to influence public policy on specific issues without seeking to become the government
A federal agency responsible for implementing government economic programmes
A judicial body that reviews government policies and strikes down unconstitutional laws
A political organization whose main aim is to contest elections and form government
questions.explanation: Pressure groups lobby and influence policy on particular issues without contesting elections to form government. A political party seeks to win elections, the judiciary reviews laws, and a federal agency implements programmes, so those options are incorrect.

questions.q: Which factor most weakens party discipline in many Nigerian political parties?
options: A clear and enforced code of conduct for party members
A strict system of internal party primaries for candidate selection
Strong loyalty to ethnic, regional or patronage networks above party directives
High levels of funding transparency and auditing within the party
questions.explanation: In Nigeria, loyalty to ethnic or patronage networks often overrides party directives, weakening discipline. Strict primaries, enforced codes, and funding transparency would strengthen rather than weaken discipline, so they are not correct.

questions.q: Which of these pressure group activities is most likely to be considered a legitimate form of political participation in Nigeria?
options: Bribing legislators to obtain favourable votes on a bill
Seizing government buildings to demand policy changes
Threatening violence to force government officials to resign
Organizing peaceful rallies to raise awareness about environmental degradation
questions.explanation: Peaceful rallies are lawful and legitimate forms of participation. Threatening violence, bribery, and seizing government property are illegal actions and not legitimate forms of political participation.

questions.q: Which power belongs exclusively to the Nigerian Senate and not to the House of Representatives?
options: Impeaching the President for gross misconduct
Initiating money bills concerning taxation and public expenditure
Amending the constitution by a two-thirds majority
Confirming presidential appointments to federal ministries and diplomatic posts
questions.explanation: The Senate has the exclusive power to confirm presidential appointments. Initiating money bills is a function of the House of Representatives; impeachment is initiated in the House and tried in the Senate; constitutional amendment requires both houses, so those options are incorrect.

questions.q: A bill in the National Assembly is considered a law only after which sequence?
options: Approved by a judiciary review before being presented to the President
Passed by the House of Representatives only and published in the official gazette
Passed by both chambers without need for presidential assent
Passed by both chambers and signed by the President (or passed again over the President's veto)
questions.explanation: In Nigeria a bill becomes law after passage by both chambers and presidential assent; if vetoed, the National Assembly can override the veto by two-thirds majority. Passage by one chamber, no need for assent, or judicial approval first are incorrect procedures.

questions.q: Which principle ensures that courts can review actions of the executive to determine whether they are lawful in Nigeria?
options: Parliamentary privilege
Legislative supremacy
Executive immunity
Judicial review
questions.explanation: Judicial review is the power of courts to examine executive actions for legality. Parliamentary privilege protects legislators, executive immunity shields certain officials from prosecution (but not lawful review), and legislative supremacy is not the basis for courts checking the executive.

questions.q: Which of the following was a common feature of military rule in Nigeria between 1966 and 1999?
options: Complete decentralization of power to state governments
Judicial appointments made solely by the National Assembly
Governments led by military officers who often suspended parts of the constitution
Frequent open multiparty elections held under international supervision
questions.explanation: Military regimes were led by officers and often suspended constitutional provisions. They did not hold regular multiparty elections, did not decentralize power, and judicial appointments were typically controlled by the ruling military authorities, not the National Assembly.

questions.q: Which event is most associated with the end of a major military regime and the transition to civilian rule in Nigeria?
options: The 1966 counter-coup that overthrew Aguiyi-Ironsi
The 1999 general election that brought Olusegun Obasanjo to the presidency
The annulment of the 1993 presidential election by the National Electoral Commission
The 1983 coup that brought Major-General Muhammadu Buhari to power
questions.explanation: The 1999 election marked the transition from military to civilian rule with Obasanjo's presidency. The 1983 coup and 1966 events were military takeovers, while the 1993 annulment was a crisis during military rule, not the transition to civilian governance.

questions.q: Which principle has most consistently guided Nigeria’s foreign policy since independence?
options: Strict neutrality in all international conflicts without mediation
Alignment exclusively with Western powers against African interests
Isolationism and refusal to participate in regional organisations
Support for African unity and anti-colonialism
questions.explanation: Nigeria has historically promoted African unity and anti-colonialism. It has not pursued isolationism; it often engages in mediation and regional organisations like ECOWAS; and it has not aligned exclusively with Western powers against African interests.

questions.q: Nigeria led the creation of ECOWAS in 1975 mainly to achieve which of the following objectives?
options: Create a military alliance to invade non-member states
Exclude former colonial powers from all regional meetings
Promote economic cooperation and collective security among West African states
Establish a single West African currency controlled by Nigeria
questions.explanation: ECOWAS was formed to encourage economic cooperation and regional stability, including collective security. It was not created to establish a Nigeria-controlled currency, launch invasions, or exclude former colonial powers from meetings, so those options are incorrect.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why public opinion polls sometimes fail to predict election outcomes in Nigeria?
options: Election results are always manipulated, so polls are irrelevant.
Pollsters deliberately publish false results to influence voters.
Public opinion never changes between the polldate and election day.
Sampling errors and difficulty reaching rural or illiterate voters can produce biased results.
questions.explanation: Sampling errors and undercoverage of rural or illiterate populations are common reasons polls mis-predict elections in Nigeria; polls reflect the sampled population, not the whole electorate. While manipulation or deliberate misreporting can occur, the central technical problem is sampling and non-response bias rather than universal deliberate falsehoods or constant manipulation of results.

questions.q: Which citizen action is most likely to increase government responsiveness at local government level in a Nigerian town?
options: Threatening to withhold market dues unless leaders resign immediately.
Relying solely on national newspapers to report local problems.
Posting anonymous complaints on social media without naming officials.
Organising a peaceful town hall meeting with written petitions presented to the local council.
questions.explanation: A peaceful town hall with written petitions creates direct, documented interaction that local councils can act on, increasing accountability. Anonymous social media posts lack formal channels; threats are unlawful and reduce cooperation; national newspapers may not prompt quick local action compared with direct local engagement.

questions.q: Which right is most directly limited when the government imposes a curfew during a state emergency in Nigeria?
options: Freedom of movement.
Right to private property.
Right to vote in a national election.
Right to a fair hearing in court.
questions.explanation: A curfew restricts citizens' ability to move freely, so it directly limits freedom of movement. It generally does not directly affect property rights, judicial hearing rights, or voting rights (which occur at separate times) unless additional extraordinary measures are taken.

questions.q: Which constitutional provision best protects the independence of the Nigerian judiciary?
options: Allowing the National Assembly to appoint judges for fixed two-year terms.
Provision for security of tenure and non-removal except by specified procedures.
Requirement that judges follow directives of the President.
Removal of judicial pay reviews to the legislature alone.
questions.explanation: Security of tenure and removal only by prescribed processes protect judges from executive or political interference, ensuring independence. Presidential directives or short fixed terms would undermine impartiality; legislative control of pay reviews alone does not ensure independence if tenure is insecure.

questions.q: Which change would be required to alter a basic feature of Nigeria’s federal structure under most constitutions?
options: An executive order by the President for national unity.
A resolution passed by the National Judicial Council.
A simple majority vote in the House of Representatives alone.
A constitutional amendment following the special procedure involving both National Assembly and state assemblies.
questions.explanation: Altering a fundamental feature of the federal structure requires a constitutional amendment with the special procedure—approval by the National Assembly and a specified number of state assemblies—so it is not done by a simple majority or executive order. The NJC has no power to change constitutional structures.

questions.q: Which principle ensures that no single organ of government has unlimited power in Nigeria's constitution?
options: Majority rule.
Precedence of customary law over the constitution.
Separation of powers.
Judicial supremacy over Parliament.
questions.explanation: Separation of powers divides authority among legislative, executive and judicial branches to prevent concentration of power. Majority rule is a democratic principle but does not by itself limit organs; judicial supremacy or precedence of customary law would concentrate, not limit, power.

questions.q: Which constitutional event in Nigeria marked the transition from a unitary to a federal system with regional assemblies?
options: The 1963 Republican Constitution.
The 1954 Lyttleton Constitution.
The 1979 Presidential Constitution.
The 1999 Constitution.
questions.explanation: The 1954 Lyttleton Constitution reorganised Nigeria into a federation with regional assemblies, moving away from a unitary colonial structure. The 1963 constitution made Nigeria a republic; 1979 and 1999 related to presidential and current arrangements but did not mark the original shift to federal regionalism.

questions.q: During constitutional discussions leading to the 1979 Constitution, which issue was most controversial among political leaders?
options: Whether to make English illegal in government business.
The form of government: parliamentary versus presidential.
Whether to adopt Nigeria as a confederation of independent states.
Choosing the national currency name instead of naira.
questions.explanation: Debate over parliamentary versus presidential systems was central in the lead-up to the 1979 Constitution; leaders disagreed on executive strength and checks. The other options are implausible extremes: confederation was not seriously proposed then, the naira was already the currency name, and banning English was not a mainstream constitutional issue.

questions.q: Which ECOWAS mechanism is designed to respond to unconstitutional changes of government among member states?
options: ECOWAS Monetary Union Stabilisation Fund.
The Protocol on Democracy and Good Governance.
ECOWAS Cultural Exchange Programme.
ECOWAS Free Trade Agreement for Goods.
questions.explanation: The Protocol on Democracy and Good Governance provides measures for responding to coups and unconstitutional changes, including sanctions and intervention. Free trade, monetary union funds, and cultural programmes do not address political crises or unconstitutional changes of government.

questions.q: Nigeria, as a large UN troop-contributing country, most directly supports UN peacekeeping by providing which of the following?
options: Permanent seats on the UN Security Council.
Exclusive control over UN funding decisions for Africa.
Automatic veto power in UN General Assembly votes.
Trained military and police units deployed under UN command.
questions.explanation: Peacekeeping contributions consist of trained military and police units deployed under UN command. Permanent Security Council seats, veto powers, and exclusive control over UN funding are not tied to troop contributions and are not conferred by providing troops.

questions.q: Which form of government is characterised by decision-making power concentrated in a small group of military officers who rule by decree, often suspending the constitution and political parties?
options: Constitutional monarchy
Parliamentary democracy
Military government
Federal republic
questions.explanation: Military government fits the description: a small group of officers rules by decree and often suspends constitutional processes. Parliamentary democracy and constitutional monarchy retain civilian institutions and parties, while a federal republic describes a division of powers between central and regional governments rather than rule by the military.

questions.q: In a presidential system, which feature distinguishes it most clearly from a parliamentary system?
options: Separation of executive and legislative branches with a fixed term for the president
Executive depends on legislative confidence to remain in office
Head of government is also head of state
Prime minister appointed from the legislature
questions.explanation: A presidential system has a clear separation of powers and a president with a fixed term. The other options describe parliamentary systems where head of government can be removed by legislative confidence and the prime minister is chosen from the legislature; in many presidential systems head of state and government are the same (the president), but that alone does not distinguish the systems as clearly as separation of branches.

questions.q: Which electoral system is most likely used when a candidate must obtain the highest number of votes in a single-member constituency to win, even if not an absolute majority?
options: Two-round system
Proportional representation
Single transferable vote
First-past-the-post (plurality) system
questions.explanation: First-past-the-post (plurality) awards victory to the candidate with the most votes in a single-member constituency, even without an absolute majority. Proportional representation and single transferable vote allocate seats to reflect overall vote shares, while a two-round system requires a second round if no candidate achieves a set threshold.

questions.q: A state electoral commission in Lagos announces results showing Candidate A 18,520 votes, Candidate B 18,513 votes, and Candidate C 2,000 votes. Candidate B demands a recount citing suspected counting errors. Under common electoral practice, which ground is strongest for ordering a recount?
options: Candidate C received votes that could change the winner
Presence of international observers at some polling units
A very small margin between leading candidates suggesting possible counting or clerical error
High turnout in urban wards compared with rural wards
questions.explanation: A tiny margin (7 votes) between the top two candidates is the strongest practical ground for a recount because minor counting or clerical mistakes could change the result. High turnout differences or presence of observers are not direct legal grounds for a recount, and Candidate C's total (2,000) does not invalidate the need for recount of close counts between A and B.

questions.q: Which feature best illustrates fiscal federalism in Nigeria?
options: Appointment of federal ministers by the president
Use of traditional rulers to collect local taxes
Creation of states by federal legislative act
Allocation of revenue between federal, state and local governments by constitutional formula
questions.explanation: Fiscal federalism concerns how revenue is raised and shared; the constitutional revenue allocation formula is central. Appointment of ministers and creation of states are political or administrative acts, while traditional rulers collecting taxes is not part of the constitutional fiscal sharing arrangement.

questions.q: Which change would most increase the autonomy of Nigerian states within the federal system?
options: Increase federal allocation to states from the federation account
Mandate uniform state laws across all states on education
Allow states to legislate on matters currently in the exclusive list, such as mining and petroleum regulation
Require states to seek federal approval before borrowing for infrastructure
questions.explanation: Allowing states to legislate on currently exclusive federal matters increases state autonomy. Requiring federal approval for borrowing or mandating uniform laws would reduce autonomy, while increasing federal allocations does not change legislative authority.

questions.q: Which source of legitimacy best explains why most Nigerians accept the authority of an elected president?
options: The president inherited power through traditional succession
The president exercises authority by force with no popular support
The president is selected by foreign powers
The president gained power through constitutionally prescribed elections accepted as fair by the electorate
questions.explanation: Legitimacy from free and accepted elections explains popular acceptance of an elected president. Inherited traditional succession, rule by force, or selection by foreigners do not provide popular democratic legitimacy in a constitutional republic like Nigeria.

questions.q: Sovereignty in the context of the Nigerian state is best described as:
options: The power of foreign investors to control local resources
The personal authority of a traditional ruler over his village
A political party’s dominance over state institutions
The supreme legal authority of the state within its territorial borders and in international relations
questions.explanation: Sovereignty refers to the state's ultimate legal authority internally and externally. Personal traditional authority, influence of investors, or party dominance are different concepts and do not define state sovereignty.

questions.q: If a governor issues an executive order within the scope of state law but the federal government claims it is unconstitutional, which body has the authority to determine the order’s legality under Nigeria’s constitutional arrangements?
options: The state legislature by simple majority vote
Traditional council of chiefs
The judiciary (courts) through judicial review
The federal executive alone without court involvement
questions.explanation: Judicial review by the courts determines constitutionality disputes between federal and state actions. The state legislature cannot alone declare an order unconstitutional; the federal executive lacks unilateral judicial authority, and traditional chiefs have no constitutional role in legal adjudication.

questions.topic: Separation of powers and checks and balances
questions.q: Which action by the Nigerian National Assembly best illustrates the principle of checks and balances over the executive?
options: A governor appointing a caretaker committee for a local council
Passing a law to increase the president's emergency powers
Rejecting a president's ministerial nomination after public hearings
The president signing a bill into law without amendments
questions.explanation: Rejecting a presidential ministerial nomination is a legislative check on the executive's appointment power. Passing a law to increase presidential powers strengthens the executive rather than checking it; the president signing a bill is an executive act within lawmaking, not a check; a governor appointing local officials is a state executive action and not a federal check on the president.

questions.topic: Separation of powers and checks and balances
questions.q: If the president refuses to sign a bill but the National Assembly overrides the refusal, this demonstrates which constitutional mechanism?
options: A constitutional referendum
Judicial review of executive action
A legislative override of an executive veto
Impeachment of the president
questions.explanation: When the legislature passes a bill again by the required majority to make it law despite presidential refusal, that is an override of the veto. Judicial review would involve courts; impeachment is removal of the president; a referendum is a popular vote to change law or constitution, not an override.

questions.topic: Separation of powers and checks and balances
questions.q: Which of the following limits the power of the judiciary in Nigeria?
options: The president dissolving the Supreme Court by executive order
Judges changing their own salaries by judicial decree
Parliament passing a constitutionally valid law that removes certain appellate jurisdiction
The judiciary issuing binding instructions to the National Assembly
questions.explanation: Parliament can, within constitutional limits, alter or limit court jurisdiction by law, which is a legislative check. Judges cannot unilaterally change their salaries (that requires other branches); the judiciary cannot direct the legislature; the president lacks power to dissolve the Supreme Court by executive order under the constitution.

questions.q: Which activity best describes the role of a pressure group in Nigeria?
options: Appointing ministers to the federal cabinet
Presenting a candidate for presidency in a general election
Lobbying the National Assembly to change a tax policy affecting farmers
Serving as the final court of appeal in disputes between states
questions.explanation: Pressure groups lobby government institutions to influence policy without seeking to win elections. Presenting presidential candidates is the role of political parties; courts adjudicate disputes; appointing ministers is an executive prerogative.

questions.q: A student association stages a peaceful rally in Abuja to demand free university tuition. This action is an example of which democratic function of pressure groups?
options: Exercising judicial review
Articulating and aggregating interests
Conducting a national election
Issuing executive orders
questions.explanation: Organizing a rally brings attention to collective interests and aggregates concerns to influence policy. Judicial review is a court function; elections are run by electoral bodies; issuing executive orders is an executive action.

questions.q: Which characteristic distinguishes a mass political party from a cadre party in Nigeria?
options: Exclusive membership limited to military officers
Functioning primarily as a pressure group without contesting elections
Large membership with broad social base and grassroots structures
Being legally forbidden from participating in elections
questions.explanation: Mass parties recruit broadly and build grassroots organizations. Cadre parties are typically smaller and elite-based, but exclusive military membership describes a military clique, not a cadre party per se. Pressure groups may not contest elections; a legal ban on contesting would not define a mass party.

questions.q: Which feature is unique to a presidential system like Nigeria's compared with a parliamentary system?
options: Ministers are directly appointed by the majority party in the legislature
The executive must resign if it loses a confidence vote in the legislature
Separation of membership between the executive and legislature (no automatic dual membership)
The head of government is always also head of state
questions.explanation: In presidential systems the executive (president) is not a member of the legislature, showing a clear separation. Being both head of state and government can occur in both systems; resignation after losing confidence is a parliamentary feature; ministers appointed by the majority party describes parliamentary practice.

questions.q: Which power is exercised by the Nigerian judiciary but not by the National Assembly?
options: Approving annual federal budgets
Appointing the president
Interpreting the constitution to resolve disputes about legality of laws
Enacting criminal statutes
questions.explanation: Judges interpret the constitution and can rule on the legality of laws and government actions. Approving budgets and enacting statutes are legislative functions; appointing the president is not a legislature power under the constitution.

questions.q: During military rule in Nigeria, which institutional change commonly replaced civilian local government councils?
options: Holding multiparty local elections supervised by the judiciary
Creation of independent, elected local assemblies with fiscal autonomy
Appointment of military administrators and caretaker committees
Transfer of local government control to traditional rulers by constitutional mandate
questions.explanation: Military regimes often appointed administrators or caretaker committees to run local councils instead of holding elections. Multiparty elections and independent elected assemblies are features of civilian democratic rule; while traditional rulers might be consulted, constitutional transfer of control to them was not the common institutional pattern.

questions.q: Which action best explains why military regimes in Nigeria often suspended parts of the constitution?
options: To permanently empower the legislature over the executive
To transfer judicial review powers to state governors
To remove legal constraints that limited executive (military) powers
To encourage immediate multiparty democratic contests
questions.explanation: Suspension of constitutional provisions allowed military rulers to exercise broad powers without legal limits. It did not transfer review powers to governors or empower legislatures; nor was it intended to promote immediate multiparty democracy, which was typically delayed under military rule.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes Nigeria's foreign policy principle of 'good neighbourliness' as practiced in West Africa?
options: Refusing cooperation with neighbours to maintain strict neutrality
Prioritising bilateral trade with distant countries over regional ties
Promoting regional stability by mediating conflicts and supporting peaceful settlements among neighbouring states
Extending unilateral military occupation to secure Nigeria’s borders
questions.explanation: Nigeria's 'good neighbourliness' means active engagement to ensure regional stability, including mediation and support for peaceful settlements. It does not justify occupation or isolation; nor is it about ignoring regional ties in favour of distant trade.

questions.q: Nigeria's leading role in the creation of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) in 1975 was primarily motivated by:
options: A plan to replace the United Nations with a regional organisation
The desire to promote economic integration and collective security among West African states
An intention to establish a single currency immediately across West Africa
A policy to limit diplomatic relations with non-African countries
questions.explanation: Nigeria supported ECOWAS to foster economic cooperation and regional security. Immediate single currency adoption was not the primary goal; ECOWAS did not aim to replace the UN or to restrict external diplomatic relations.

questions.q: When Nigeria contributes troops to a UN peacekeeping operation, the action most directly reflects which foreign policy objective?
options: Promoting international peace and enhancing Nigeria’s diplomatic influence
Establishing military bases for long-term regional control
Preventing neighbouring countries from joining the UN
Securing exclusive economic rights in the host country
questions.explanation: Contributing troops to UN missions signals commitment to global peace and raises Nigeria’s diplomatic standing. It is not meant to secure exclusive economic rights, establish long-term bases, or block UN membership for others.

questions.q: Which of the following actions is an example of civic participation by Nigerian citizens in influencing public policy?
options: Refusing to obey traffic laws because of a political disagreement
Joining a peaceful lobby to urge the Lagos State government to improve public transport
Withdrawing all money from banks during a national election
Using violent confrontation to force a policy change
questions.explanation: Joining a peaceful lobby is a legitimate form of civic participation to influence policy. Withdrawing money or illegal/violent actions are not legitimate or constructive means of influencing public policy.

questions.q: Public opinion polls in Nigeria show 60% support for a policy change. Which statement about using this result to make government decisions is most accurate?
options: Minority opinions are irrelevant when a majority is identified
The government must immediately adopt the policy because majority support is legally binding
Poll results are always unreliable and should be ignored completely
Policymakers should consider the poll as one input but also evaluate minority views, expert advice and practical feasibility
questions.explanation: Public opinion is an important input but not the sole basis for decisions; other factors matter. Majority support in a poll is not legally binding, polls are not always useless, and minority views can be important.

questions.q: Which right is most directly linked to citizenship and allows Nigerians to seek to change an unjust law peacefully?
options: The right to appoint judges directly
The right to expropriate private property without compensation
The right to absolute immunity from prosecution
The right to freedom of assembly and petition
questions.explanation: Freedom of assembly and petition enables citizens to gather and request changes to laws. The other options are not rights associated with ordinary citizenship and are inconsistent with constitutional norms.

questions.q: A constitution that sets out the distribution of powers between federal and state governments and can be changed only by a special procedure is best described as:
options: An unwritten flexible constitution
A customary law code
A written, rigid constitution
A provisional ordinance
questions.explanation: A written, rigid constitution is codified and requires special procedures for amendment. An unwritten flexible constitution would not be codified or difficult to amend; customary law and provisional ordinances are not constitutional frameworks of that description.

questions.q: Which constitutional device allows the Nigerian National Assembly to override a governor's veto on a bill passed by a state House of Assembly?
options: An emergency constitutional council that nullifies state vetoes
A national judicial override clause applicable to states
There is no device allowing the National Assembly to override a state governor's veto on state legislation
A federal override power exercised by the president
questions.explanation: Nigeria’s federal structure separates federal and state legislative powers; the National Assembly cannot override a state governor’s veto on state laws. The other options describe powers that do not exist under Nigeria’s constitution.

questions.q: Which constitutional change occurred with the 1979 Constitution in Nigeria?
options: Abolition of states and return to provinces
Introduction of the presidential system replacing the parliamentary system
Declaration of Sharia law as the supreme law for the whole country
Adoption of a single-party state as permanent system
questions.explanation: The 1979 Constitution established a presidential system replacing the parliamentary system. It did not create a permanent single-party state, abolish states, or impose Sharia nationwide.

questions.q: The adoption of the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria was significant because it:
options: Removed the office of the presidency in favour of a council of generals
Marked the transition from military rule to an elected civilian government
Converted Nigeria into a confederation of independent states
Established military rule as the permanent form of government
questions.explanation: The 1999 Constitution restored civilian democratic rule after military rule. It did not entrench military rule, abolish the presidency, or convert Nigeria into a confederation.

questions.q: Which organ of the United Nations has primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security and can authorise peacekeeping missions that Nigeria might join?
options: Security Council
General Assembly
Economic and Social Council
International Court of Justice
questions.explanation: The UN Security Council is charged with maintaining international peace and security and can authorise peacekeeping operations and sanctions. The General Assembly can discuss and recommend but cannot authorise enforcement measures; ECOSOC deals with economic and social matters; the ICJ settles legal disputes between states but does not authorise peacekeeping.

questions.q: ECOWAS intervened in West African crises in the 1990s and 2000s. Which principle or instrument of ECOWAS most directly justifies military interventions to restore democratic order in member states?
options: Convention on Mutual Legal Assistance
ECOWAS Trade Liberalisation Scheme
Protocol on Democracy and Good Governance
Protocol on Free Movement of Persons
questions.explanation: The Protocol on Democracy and Good Governance provides ECOWAS the mandate to respond to unconstitutional changes of government, including regional intervention. The trade, legal assistance and free movement instruments address economic, judicial or migration issues and do not provide a direct basis for military intervention.

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes the African Union's approach to unconstitutional changes of government from the older Organisation of African Unity policy of non-interference?
options: The AU allows suspension of member states after coups and can impose sanctions
The AU requires previous coloniser approval before suspending a state
The AU always sends UN peacekeepers to restore civilian rule
The AU treats all military governments as legitimate without conditions
questions.explanation: Unlike the OAU's strict non-interference, the AU adopted a stance that permits suspending members after unconstitutional changes and using measures like sanctions to restore constitutional order. The AU does not automatically deploy UN peacekeepers, does not legitimise all military governments, and does not require former coloniser approval.

questions.q: Which feature is most characteristic of a presidential system of government as practised in Nigeria?
options: Separation of executive and legislative branches with direct election of the president
Executive is collectively responsible to the legislature
Head of state is a hereditary monarch
Prime minister is chosen from the majority party in the legislature
questions.explanation: A presidential system features separation of powers and a president directly elected by voters, as in Nigeria. Choosing a prime minister from the legislature and collective responsibility describe parliamentary systems; a hereditary monarch defines a monarchy, not Nigeria's republican presidency.

questions.q: Which form of government concentrates decision-making in the hands of a single leader or small group, often suspending civil liberties and political opposition?
options: Confederal system
Liberal democracy
Authoritarian regime
Federal republic
questions.explanation: Authoritarian regimes centralise power and often suppress opposition and civil liberties. Liberal democracy protects rights and competitive politics; confederal and federal systems describe territorial arrangements, not the concentration of personal power implied by authoritarianism.

questions.q: Which advantage is commonly claimed for a parliamentary system compared with a presidential system?
options: Direct election of head of state by national popular vote
Stronger separation between executive and legislature
Greater likelihood of swift removal of ineffective executives by a vote of no confidence
Fixed term limits that prevent early changes of government
questions.explanation: Parliamentary systems allow the legislature to remove a government quickly via a vote of no confidence. Strong separation of branches and fixed terms are features of presidential systems; direct popular election of head of state is typical of presidential systems, not parliamentary ones where head of government is usually chosen by parliament.

questions.q: Which electoral system tends to produce single-party majority governments and is used for many single-member constituencies for the National Assembly in Nigeria?
options: Mixed-member proportional representation
Party-list proportional representation
First-past-the-post (plurality) system
Single transferable vote
questions.explanation: First-past-the-post in single-member constituencies often gives larger parties a majority of seats and is used for many Nigerian legislative contests. Party-list PR and STV are proportional systems producing more balanced seat distributions; mixed-member proportional combines both and is not Nigeria's standard for most constituencies.

questions.q: Which constitutional feature helps to protect smaller or less populous states in Nigeria within the federal system?
options: A single national legislature with no upper chamber
Residency requirement preventing inter-state movement
Direct appointment of state governors by the president
Equal representation of states in the Senate
questions.explanation: Equal state representation in the Senate gives all states similar influence regardless of population, protecting smaller states. Presidential appointment of governors would undermine state autonomy, a single chamber would remove that protective balance, and residency restrictions would not be a constitutional protection for small states.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common advantage of federalism for a country like Nigeria?
options: It eliminates all regional differences through centralised planning
It guarantees equal wealth for all states regardless of resources
It allows regions to make policies reflecting local conditions and preferences
It prevents any national government from collecting taxes
questions.explanation: Federalism lets sub-national units tailor policies to local needs, an advantage in diverse countries like Nigeria. Federalism does not eliminate regional differences, guarantee equal wealth, or stop the national government from taxing; rather it shares powers and revenue between levels.

questions.topic: Separation of powers and checks and balances
questions.q: Which of the following is the best example of the judicial branch checking the power of the executive in Nigeria?
options: The President appoints new judges to the Federal High Court to speed up cases involving the executive.
The President refuses to sign a bill passed by the National Assembly and returns it for reconsideration.
The Senate rejects the President’s nominee for a federal ministerial post.
A Federal High Court declares a presidential directive to be inconsistent with the Constitution and null and void.
questions.explanation: When a court declares a presidential directive unconstitutional and void, the judiciary is exercising judicial review to limit executive action. The Senate rejecting a nominee is a legislative check on the executive, not a judicial one. The President refusing to sign a bill is an executive action (a veto/withholding of assent) and not a judicial check. The President appointing judges is an executive power and could undermine judicial independence rather than being a check by the judiciary.

questions.q: During periods of military rule in Nigeria (e.g. 1966–1979, 1983–1999), which institutional change was most commonly implemented by the ruling juntas?
options: Suspension of the constitution and rule by military decrees
Strengthening judicial independence and review powers
Expansion of the powers of the National Assembly
Introduction of unrestricted multiparty elections
questions.explanation: Military regimes in Nigeria routinely suspended the constitution and governed by military orders and decrees; this allowed the juntas to centralise authority. The other options are incorrect because juntas did not promote free multiparty contests, they reduced the legislature's authority rather than expanding it, and they often weakened judicial independence instead of strengthening it.
